meta.title: Who really said "Facts are stubborn things"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: John Adams said it in his 1770 Boston Massacre defense, and it was printed that year. But he didn't coin it. The proverb is documented decades earlier.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Facts are stubborn things'?
meta.ogDescription: Adams really said it, in his Dec. 1770 closing for the Boston Massacre soldiers, printed that year. The proverb itself is older: the earliest form found is from 1713.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: From Adams’s closing argument for the British soldiers at the Boston Massacre trial (3–4 December 1770). It was printed that year in The Trial of William Wemms…, taken down in shorthand by John Hodgson (Boston: J. Fleeming, 1770). The wording is confirmed in a scan of that edition. Adams quoted an existing proverb. He did not invent it.

source.excerpt: I will enlarge no more on the evidence, but submit it to you.—Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes, our inclinations, or the dictates of our passions, they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence: nor is the law less stable than the fact;
trail: The 1770 shorthand report of the trial ↗ (Boston: J. Fleeming) contains the passage. It comes after the reporter’s note that Adams “concluded.”
The Massachusetts Historical Society’s Legal Papers of John Adams ↗ dates the argument to 3–4 December 1770. Its text is taken from that printed trial report.
Quote Investigator ↗ accepts that Adams used the phrase in his 1770 defense. It also shows that the proverb was already in print by 1713.
Wikiquote ↗ lists the line among Adams’s quotes from the Boston Massacre trial.
source.excerptNote: From the 1770 printed report, with the long ‘s’ (‘ftubborn’, ‘paffions’) changed to modern spelling. In the report, the shorthand reporter sums up most of Adams’s review of the evidence and then gives his last words in full, starting from this point. Many modern versions print “passion” in the singular, but the 1770 text has “passions.”

source.rightsNote: The line was first published in The Trial of William Wemms… (Boston: J. Fleeming, 1770), well before 1931, so the wording is in the public domain in the United States. A modern scholarly edition’s editorial notes may carry their own rights, but Adams’s words do not.

author.metaLine: 1735–1826 · Massachusetts lawyer, revolutionary & 2nd President of the United States
author.bio: A Boston lawyer before he was a revolutionary, John Adams agreed in 1770 to defend the British soldiers charged over the Boston Massacre, and the case was very unpopular in the town. He went on to serve in the Continental Congress, as a diplomat in Europe, as the first Vice President and as the second President of the United States.

misattribution.heading: Said by Adams, coined by someone else
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Adams is real. The common mix-up is the idea that he invented the saying. He was using a proverb that was already around, and quote books have named other people as its source.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ found a close version, “matters of fact are stubborn things,” in Treason Unmask’d (1713). It also found the exact phrase in The Political State of Great Britain (November 1717). Both come before Adams’s 1770 argument.

Quote Investigator ↗ reports that Bartlett’s Familiar Quotations (10th edition, 1919) gave the line to Smollett’s translation of Lesage’s Gil Blas, not to Adams. Bartlett’s own footnote pointed to an earlier source, from 1747.

In his 15 August 1988 convention speech ↗, Reagan said, “as John Adams said, ‘Facts are stubborn things.’” Later in the same speech he slipped: “Facts are stupid things—stubborn things, I should say.” The slip is quoted on its own so often that it is sometimes mistaken for the source.

misattribution.truthLine: John Adams did say “Facts are stubborn things,” in his December 1770 defense of the Boston Massacre soldiers, as the 1770 printed trial report ↗ shows. But he was quoting a proverb that, according to Quote Investigator ↗, was already in print by 1713.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In March 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd in Boston and killed five men, including Crispus Attucks. The soldiers were put on trial for murder in a town that was furious with them. Adams took on their defense. He ended his closing argument by asking the jury to put feelings aside and judge on the evidence and the law, and this line was the turning point of that ending.

Adams used the proverb to say that the jury’s wishes, inclinations and passions could not change what the witnesses had shown. He then argued that the law was just as fixed: if the soldiers were attacked, the law allowed self-defense, or at least reduced the charge to manslaughter.
context.pull: Facts are stubborn things; and whatever may be our wishes… they cannot alter the state of facts and evidence.
